hints: Look carefully at what the y-axis is telling you. Where on the graph is the spindle fibre length at its longest, where is it shortening, and where has it reached zero?

Remember when centromeres are attached to spindle fibres. They attach in prometaphase, stay attached at metaphase and during pulling in anaphase, and only lose all attachment when the spindle breaks down in telophase.
walkthrough:
**Read the shape of the graph**

Think of this curve as the life story of the spindle. It grows longer, stays at maximum length for a short time, then gets shorter, then disappears to zero.

Longer means spindle microtubules are polymerising and reaching out. Shorter means they are depolymerising as they pull.

**Match shape to stages of mitosis**

Region A (rising): prophase to prometaphase, spindle forms and centromeres attach. Region B (flat top): metaphase, all chromosomes lined up on the equator with centromeres attached and spindle at full length.

Region C (falling): anaphase, centromeres have divided and spindle fibres shorten to pull sister chromatids apart. Attachment is still present here.

**Find when all detachment has happened**

Centromeres can only be fully free when there is no spindle left to hold them. That is region D, where length has fallen to zero.

This is late telophase, after pulling is finished and the spindle is disassembled, so all centromeres have detached.

options.A: Region A is spindle formation and attachment, not detachment. Centromeres are just attaching to the growing spindle here.
options.B: Region B is metaphase at maximum length. All centromeres are firmly attached to spindle fibres at the equator.
options.C: Region C is anaphase shortening. Centromeres (now on separate chromatids) are still attached while being pulled to opposite poles.
options.D: Region D shows spindle length at zero. The spindle has broken down in telophase, so all centromeres have detached.
